title: Can Foreign Hackers Really Change Your Vote? What Experts Say About Voting Machine Security
summary: Imagine casting your vote, but a hacker far away changes it without you knowing. Scary, right? A US official named Markwayne Mullin recently said that foreign adversaries can definitely access voting machines and change votes. He claimed it's not even up for debate. But is that true? Experts say voting machines do have security holes. A professor named J. Alex Halderman once showed how hackers could reprogram a machine to make any candidate win—if they got physical access to it. But in real elections, machines are locked up, watched by cameras, and kept offline. So it's much harder to attack them. The good news? There's no evidence that any foreign enemy has ever used these weaknesses to mess with a real US election. A 2021 report from intelligence agencies found no proof of vote manipulation in 2020. Plus, most states now use paper ballots that you mark by hand. That means officials can recount them to double-check the results. Andrew Appel, another expert, says today's voting machines are more secure than older ones. But the risk isn't zero. That's why election workers test machines before elections and keep them safe. So while the idea of vote hacking sounds terrifying, the reality is that many layers of protection make it very unlikely. Still, experts say we should keep improving security—just in case.
why_it_matters: Your right to vote is protected by many layers of security, so it’s important to understand how elections are kept safe.

background_read: Voting machines have been debated in US elections for years. After the 2020 election, many claims of hacked machines were investigated and found no evidence of changed votes.
Every state runs its own elections with different systems. After 2020, more states switched to paper ballots and stronger testing to make elections safer.

perspectives.description: They argue that foreign hackers could access voting machines, so the country must stay alert and fix weaknesses.
They admit machines have flaws but emphasize that real attacks are very difficult because machines are locked up, never online, and backed up by paper.
They trust the current systems because of testing and physical security, but they always work to improve protections.
